Q1. BERT vs GPT vs T5, and Parameter Count of a Decoder-only Transformer
Compare BERT, GPT, and T5 in terms of architecture, pre-training objectives, and typical
applications. Consider a decoder-only Transformer with n = 24 layers, hidden dimension
d = 2048, h = 16 attention heads, feed-forward dimension df f = 8192, and parameters per
layer Player = 12d

Part 1: Comparison of BERT, GPT and T5
All three are built from the Transformer block (multi-head self-attention + position-wise feed￾forward network + residual connections + layer normalization), but they use different parts of the
original encoder–decoder Transformer and are trained with different objectives.
1. BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers)
• Architecture: Encoder-only stack. Self-attention is bidirectional: every token attends to all
tokens to its left and right. BERT-Base: 12 layers, d = 768, 12 heads, 110M parameters; BERT￾Large: 24 layers, d = 1024, 16 heads, 340M parameters.
• Pre-training objectives:
(i) Masked Language Modelling (MLM): 15% of input tokens are selected; of these 80% are
replaced by [MASK], 10% by a random token and 10% left unchanged. The model predicts
the original tokens: LMLM = −

and x˜ is the corrupted input.
(ii) Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): binary classification of whether sentence B actually follows
sentence A.
• Typical applications: Natural language understanding tasks – text classification, sentiment
analysis, named entity recognition, extractive question answering (SQuAD), semantic similarity,
embeddings for search/retrieval. It is not naturally suited for free-form text generation.
2. GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer)
• Architecture: Decoder-only stack with causal (masked) self-attention: token t can attend only
to tokens 1, . . . , t. There is no encoder and no cross-attention.
• Pre-training objective: Causal (autoregressive) language modelling – predict the next token:
LCLM = −

• Typical applications: Natural language generation – chatbots, story/essay writing, code gener￾ation, summarization, translation, and (from GPT-3 onwards) zero-shot and few-shot in-context
learning of many tasks through prompting.
3. T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer)
• Architecture: Full encoder–decoder Transformer. The encoder is bidirectional; the decoder is
causal and also uses cross-attention over the encoder outputs. Uses relative position biases.
• Pre-training objective: Span corruption (a denoising objective). Random contiguous spans
of the input are replaced by sentinel tokens <X>, <Y>, . . . , and the decoder generates the missing
spans.
Example: Input: “Thank you <X> me to your party <Y> week.” Target: “<X> for inviting <Y>
last <Z>”.

Homework: LLM and its Application – Solutions Page 4
• Key idea: Every task is cast as text-to-text: a task prefix is prepended to the input (e.g.
“translate English to German: . . . ”, “summarize: . . . ”) and the output is always text.
• Typical applications: Translation, summarization, question answering, classification (output
label as text) – any sequence-to-sequence task.

Q2. Emergent Abilities and Data Scaling Laws
What are emergent abilities in LLMs? Explain how scaling can lead to the emergence of new
capabilities, with examples. An LLM is trained on Dataset A (100 billion tokens) and Dataset
B (400 billion tokens). Loss follows L(D) = 
Dc
D
αD
with αD = 0.5. (a) Ratio LB/LA. (b)
LB if LA = 2.0. (c) Significance of scaling laws in planning LLM training.
Part 1: Emergent abilities
Definition: An ability is called emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger
models. On a plot of task performance versus model scale (parameters, data or training compute),
performance stays near random chance for small models and then rises sharply and unpredictably
once the scale crosses a certain threshold. Such abilities cannot be predicted by simply extrapolating
the performance of smaller models.
How scaling leads to emergence:
1. Smooth loss, sharp task metrics. The next-token loss decreases smoothly (as a power law)
with scale. Many tasks, however, need several sub-skills to all be correct at once (e.g. every step
of a multi-step calculation). If each step is correct with probability p, a k-step task succeeds
with probability p
k
. As p improves gradually, p
k
stays near zero for a long time and then rises
rapidly, which appears as a sudden jump.
2. Exact-match metrics. Metrics such as exact match give zero credit to partially correct answers,
so gradual improvement is hidden until answers become fully correct.
3. Capacity for richer representations. Larger models trained on more diverse data store more
world knowledge and learn more abstract internal representations (e.g. of arithmetic, syntax,
logical structure) that can be combined to solve new tasks.
4. Diverse data. Very large corpora contain implicit demonstrations of many tasks (Q&A pairs,
translations, worked solutions), which large models can absorb and later reuse.
Examples of emergent abilities:
• In-context (few-shot) learning: GPT-3 (175B) can learn a new task from a few examples in
the prompt without weight updates; much smaller GPT models could not do this reliably.
• Chain-of-thought reasoning: Prompting with step-by-step reasoning improves multi-step
arithmetic (e.g. GSM8K) only for models of roughly 60–100B parameters and above; for small
models it does not help or even hurts.
• Multi-digit arithmetic: 3-digit addition/subtraction accuracy jumps from near zero to high
accuracy at large scale.
• Instruction following: Large instruction-tuned models generalize to unseen instructions, while
small models do not.
• Others: word unscrambling, transliteration, code generation from natural language descriptions,
multi-task language understanding (MMLU) above chance.

(c) Significance of scaling laws in planning LLM training
1. Predictability: Scaling laws express loss as a power law in model size N, data size D and
compute C, e.g. L(N) = (Nc/N)
αN , L(D) = (Dc/D)
αD . Small, cheap experiments can be fitted
and extrapolated to predict the loss of a very large run before spending millions on it.
2. Optimal allocation of compute: For a fixed compute budget (C ≈ 6ND FLOPs), scaling laws
decide how to split the budget between model size and data. The Chinchilla study (Hoffmann et
al., 2022) showed that N and D should be scaled roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter;
earlier models such as GPT-3 were under-trained on data.
3. Data requirement estimation: As in parts (a)–(b), they tell us how much additional data is
needed to reach a target loss (here 4× data ⇒ loss halves when αD = 0.5).
4. Diminishing returns: Because of the power law, each further reduction in loss needs a multi￾plicative increase in resources. This helps decide when further scaling is no longer cost-effective.
5. Hardware and budget planning: Estimates of GPU count, training time, cost and energy
can be made in advance.
6. Hyper-parameter and architecture decisions: Learning rate, batch size and depth/width
choices can be tuned at small scale and transferred to large scale.
7. Risk reduction: Reduces the chance of a failed or wasteful large training run.

Q3. LLM Training Pipeline, Llama 2 Architecture, and Memory Requirements
Explain the complete training pipeline of a modern LLM. Explain the major architectural
modifications introduced in Llama 2 compared with the conventional Transformer. Llama 2
comes in 7B, 13B and 70B configurations; FP16 precision. (a) Memory to store each model. (b)
Additional memory for 70B vs 7B. (c) Which models fit on a 24 GB GPU (parameter storage
only)? (d) Why is actual GPU memory higher than parameter storage?
Part 1: Complete training pipeline of a modern LLM
1. Data collection
& cleaning
2. Tokenization
(BPE / Sen￾tencePiece)
3. Pre-training
(next-token
prediction)
4. Supervised
fine-tuning (SFT)
5. Reward model

1. Data collection and pre-processing: Trillions of tokens are gathered from web crawls (e.g.
Common Crawl), books, Wikipedia, scientific papers, and code. The data is cleaned: de￾duplication, language identification, quality filtering, removal of toxic content and personal in￾formation, and mixing of sources in suitable proportions.
2. Tokenization: Text is split into sub-word tokens using Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or Sen￾tencePiece and mapped to integer IDs from a fixed vocabulary (Llama 2 uses a 32,000-token
SentencePiece vocabulary).
3. Pre-training (self-supervised): A decoder-only Transformer is trained to predict the next
token by minimizing the cross-entropy loss L = −
P
t
log Pθ(xt
| x<t). This is the most expensive
stage (thousands of GPUs for weeks) and uses data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, mixed
precision, and the AdamW optimizer with learning-rate warm-up and cosine decay. The result
is a base model that has broad knowledge but does not reliably follow instructions.
4. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) / instruction tuning: The base model is fine-tuned on
high-quality (prompt, response) pairs written by humans, so that it learns to follow instructions
and conversational format. The loss is computed only on response tokens.
5. Reward model training: For each prompt, multiple model responses are ranked by human
annotators. A reward model rϕ(x, y) is trained so that preferred responses get higher scores
(Bradley–Terry loss, see Q4).
6. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF): The SFT model (policy) is
optimized with PPO to maximize the reward while a KL-divergence penalty keeps it close to the
SFT model. Alternatives: rejection-sampling fine-tuning (used in Llama 2 together with PPO)
or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
7. Evaluation and safety testing: Benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, TruthfulQA,
etc.), human evaluation of helpfulness and harmlessness, and red-teaming for safety.
8. Optimization and deployment: Quantization (INT8/INT4), distillation, KV-cache and batch￾ing optimizations, serving behind an API, followed by continuous monitoring and feedback col￾lection.

Only the Llama 2 7B model can theoretically fit on a 24 GB GPU in FP16. The 13B and 70B
models would need quantization (e.g. INT8/INT4) or multiple GPUs.
(d) Why actual GPU memory consumption is higher than parameter storage
1. Activations: Intermediate outputs of every layer (attention scores, FFN outputs) must be held
in memory during the forward pass; in training they are stored for back-propagation. They grow
with batch size and sequence length; attention scores grow as O(n
2
) in sequence length n.
2. KV cache (inference): During autoregressive generation, keys and values of all previous tokens
are cached for every layer. Size ≈ 2 × nlayers × ntokens × d × batch × bytes; for long contexts and
large batches this can be several GB.
3. Gradients (training): One gradient per parameter, i.e. the same size as the weights again (2
bytes/parameter in FP16).
4. Optimizer states (training): Adam stores first and second moments, usually in FP32, plus
an FP32 master copy of weights: about 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 extra bytes per parameter. Full mixed￾precision training therefore needs about 16 bytes/parameter (e.g. 7B × 16 ≈ 112 GB).
5. Framework and CUDA overhead: CUDA context, cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels and workspaces,
typically several hundred MB to 1–2 GB.
6. Memory fragmentation: The memory allocator reserves blocks that are not fully used.
7. Temporary buffers and input batches: Token IDs, embeddings, logits over the vocabulary
(batch × n × V ), and communication buffers in multi-GPU setups.

The KL penalty (weighted by β) prevents the policy from drifting too far from the SFT model,
which avoids reward hacking (producing text that fools the reward model) and preserves fluency.
Why RLHF is important for alignment:
1. Objective mismatch: Pre-training only maximizes likelihood of internet text; it does not ask
for helpful, truthful or safe answers. RLHF optimizes directly for what humans prefer.

Homework: LLM and its Application – Solutions Page 12
2. Hard-to-specify goals: Qualities like “helpful”, “polite” or “not harmful” are difficult to write
as a loss function, but humans can easily compare two answers. RLHF turns these comparisons
into a learnable reward.
3. Safety: Reduces toxic, biased and dangerous outputs and teaches the model to refuse harmful
requests.
4. Honesty: Reduces hallucination and encourages the model to express uncertainty.
5. Better instruction following: InstructGPT (1.3B) trained with RLHF was preferred by hu￾mans over the 175B GPT-3, showing alignment can matter more than size.
6. Learning from the whole response: Unlike token-level SFT, the reward evaluates the com￾plete response, so the model learns sequence-level qualities such as coherence and usefulness.

Q5. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting
What is CoT prompting? How does breaking a problem into intermediate steps improve rea￾soning? Problem: A company has 240 employees; 35% are in research; of the remaining, 40%
are in development; the rest are in administration. Find the number in each department. (a)
Direct prompting. (b) Formulate a CoT prompt. (c) Show the reasoning steps and calculate.
(d) Compare direct and CoT prompting.
Part 1: Chain-of-Thought prompting
Definition: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting is a prompting technique in which the LLM is
encouraged to generate a sequence of intermediate natural-language reasoning steps before giving
the final answer (Wei et al., 2022). It can be done in two ways:
• Few-shot CoT: The prompt contains a few example questions whose answers include worked￾out step-by-step reasoning.
• Zero-shot CoT: A trigger phrase such as “Let’s think step by step” is added to the question
(Kojima et al., 2022).
Why intermediate steps improve performance:
1. Decomposition: A complex problem is split into simpler sub-problems, each of which the model
can solve reliably.
2. More computation per answer: An LLM spends a fixed amount of computation per generated
token. Writing out the reasoning gives the model more tokens, hence more computation, before
it commits to an answer.
3. Working memory: Intermediate results (e.g. 84, 156) are written into the context, so later
steps can attend to them instead of holding everything implicitly in hidden states.
4. Matches training data: Text such as textbooks and worked solutions contains step-by-step
explanations, so this style triggers patterns the model has already learned.
5. Error reduction and checking: Each step is conditioned on correct earlier steps, which reduces
compounding errors, and the visible steps can be checked.
6. CoT is most beneficial for arithmetic word problems, commonsense and symbolic reasoning,
and multi-hop questions; the benefit is an emergent ability that appears mainly in large models
(roughly 100B parameters and above).
Part 2: Application to the given problem
(a) Direct prompting
In direct (standard) prompting, the question is given and the model is asked for only the final
answer, with no intermediate reasoning.
Example direct prompt:
Q: A company has 240 employees. Of these, 35% are working in the research
department. Among the remaining employees, 40% are working in the development
department. The rest are working in administration. Give only the final number
of employees in each department.
A:
The model must map the question to the answer in a single step, internally computing 35% of 240,
the remainder, 40% of the remainder (not of 240), and the rest. Typical errors in direct mode are:

computing 40% of the total 240 (giving 96) instead of the remaining employees, or subtracting the
percentages (100%−35%−40% = 25%) and wrongly giving administration as 60. Because no steps
are shown, such an error cannot be traced.
(b) Chain-of-Thought prompt
Few-shot CoT prompt (one worked example + the target question):
Q: A school has 200 students. 30% play football. Of the remaining students, 50%
play cricket. The rest play no sport. How many students are in each group?
A: Let’s solve step by step.
Step 1: Football = 30% of 200 = 0.30 x 200 = 60.
Step 2: Remaining = 200 - 60 = 140.
Step 3: Cricket = 50% of 140 = 0.50 x 140 = 70.
Step 4: No sport = 140 - 70 = 70.
Step 5: Check: 60 + 70 + 70 = 200. Correct.
Final answer: Football = 60, Cricket = 70, No sport = 70.

Advantages of LoRA over full fine-tuning (any two required):
1. Far fewer trainable parameters and less memory: Gradients and optimizer states are
needed only for A and B (less than 1% of the weights), so GPU memory for training drops by
up to about 3× and large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.
2. Small storage and easy task switching: Each task needs to store only the small A, B
matrices (a few MB) instead of a full model copy (many GB). One frozen base model can serve
many tasks by swapping adapters.
3. No extra inference latency: BA can be merged into W0 after training, unlike adapter layers
that add extra computation.
4. Less catastrophic forgetting and over-fitting: The original weights stay unchanged, pre￾serving general knowledge, and the low-rank constraint acts as a regularizer on small datasets.
5. Comparable quality: On many benchmarks LoRA matches the accuracy of full fine-tuning.

How it measures predictive performance:
• Interpretation as branching factor: A perplexity of k means the model is, on average, as
uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among k equally likely tokens at each step.

• Normalization: Dividing by N makes the score independent of the sequence length, so different
sequences can be compared.
• Limitations: Comparisons are valid only on the same test set with the same tokenizer/vocab￾ulary; low perplexity does not guarantee factual correctness or usefulness in downstream tasks.

Q8. Multimodal LLMs and CLIP
Explain multimodal LLMs and the need for cross-modal learning. Explain how CLIP integrates
image and text representations. System A: text in → text out. System B: text + image in →
text out. Query: “What objects are present in this image, and what is the relationship between
them?” with an image of a person riding a bicycle. (a) How each system handles the query. (b)
Compare capabilities and limitations.
Part 1: Multimodal LLMs and cross-modal learning
Multimodal LLM (MLLM): A large language model that can take inputs from (and sometimes
produce outputs in) more than one modality – text, images, audio, video – and reason over them
jointly. Examples: GPT-4V/GPT-4o, Gemini, LLaVA, Flamingo, BLIP-2, Claude.
Typical architecture:
1. Modality encoder: e.g. a Vision Transformer (ViT) or CLIP image encoder that converts an
image into a set of feature vectors (patch embeddings).
2. Projection / connector: A linear layer, MLP, Q-Former (BLIP-2) or cross-attention (Flamingo)
that maps visual features into the LLM’s token-embedding space (“visual tokens”).
3. LLM backbone: The visual tokens are placed alongside text tokens; the LLM attends over
both and generates the text answer.
4. Training: (i) alignment pre-training on image–caption pairs, (ii) visual instruction tuning on
image-question-answer data.
Need for cross-modal learning:
• Real-world information is multimodal: documents with charts, photographs, medical scans,
videos, screenshots – text alone cannot capture them.
• Grounding: Linking words to their visual referents (the word “bicycle” to the pixels of a bicycle)
gives language a grounded meaning and reduces hallucination about visual content.
• Complementary information: One modality fills gaps in the other (e.g. an image shows
spatial relations, text gives context and intent).
• New tasks: Visual question answering, image captioning, text-to-image retrieval, OCR and
document understanding, accessibility (describing images for visually impaired users).
• Shared representation: A joint embedding space allows comparison and transfer between
modalities, enabling zero-shot recognition.

space for images and text using 400 million (image, caption) pairs from the internet.

(a) How each system handles the query

2. Projection: The connector maps these features into visual tokens in the LLM embedding space.
3. Fusion: Visual tokens and the text question tokens are processed together; self-attention (or

4. Generation: The LLM generates a grounded answer, e.g.: “The image contains a person and
a bicycle (with possible background objects such as a road or trees). The person is riding the
bicycle: seated on the saddle, hands on the handlebars, feet on the pedals. So the relationship is

Major developments in GPT-3:
1. Massive scale: 175 billion parameters, 96 layers, dmodel = 12288, 96 heads, trained on about
300 billion tokens – validating the scaling laws.
2. In-context learning (ICL): The central contribution (paper title: “Language Models are Few￾Shot Learners”). Tasks are specified entirely in the prompt:
• Zero-shot: only a task description (“Translate English to French: cheese ⇒”).
• One-shot: description + one example.
• Few-shot: description + several (10–100) examples within the context window.
3. Architecture: Same decoder-only design as GPT-2 (pre-normalization), with alternating dense
and locally banded sparse attention patterns (as in the Sparse Transformer), and context doubled
to 2048 tokens.
4. Better data: Common Crawl filtered with a quality classifier, fuzzy de-duplication, and a
weighted mix in which high-quality sources (books, Wikipedia) are sampled more often.
5. Performance: Few-shot GPT-3 was competitive with fine-tuned models on several benchmarks
(e.g. TriviaQA, LAMBADA), could do 2–3 digit arithmetic, word unscrambling, and generate
news articles that humans found hard to distinguish from human-written ones.
6. Paradigm shift: From “one fine-tuned model per task” to “one general model, prompted for
many tasks”, delivered through an API.
Part 2: Why GPT-3 performs tasks without task-specific fine-tuning
1. Meta-learning during pre-training: Next-token prediction on a huge, diverse corpus implic￾itly exposes the model to countless tasks (translations, Q&A, lists, code, summaries) embedded
in natural text. To predict well, the model must learn to recognize what task a piece of text is
performing and continue it. The paper calls this the “outer loop” of learning (gradient descent
during pre-training) and the “inner loop” (in-context learning at inference).

Homework: LLM and its Application – Solutions Page 25
2. In-context learning through attention: At inference, the examples in the prompt act as
conditioning information. The attention mechanism lets the model detect the input–output
pattern in the examples and apply it to the new query, without changing any weights. Formally
the model computes P(y | task description,(x1, y1), . . . ,(xk, yk), xquery).
3. Scale: ICL is an emergent ability – the gap between zero-shot and few-shot performance grows
with model size and is largest for the 175B model; small models benefit little from examples.
4. Universal text interface: Every task can be expressed as text-in, text-out, so the same next￾token predictor can perform classification, translation, QA, etc.
5. Broad knowledge stored in parameters: 175B parameters store extensive world and lin￾guistic knowledge that can be retrieved by an appropriate prompt.
Part 3: Why instruction tuning improves instruction following
Instruction tuning is supervised fine-tuning of a pre-trained LLM on a large collection of tasks
written as natural-language instructions paired with desired outputs, e.g. (“Summarize the following
paragraph in one sentence: . . . ”, summary). Examples: FLAN, T0, InstructGPT (SFT stage),
Alpaca.
Why it helps:
1. Fixes objective mismatch: A base model is trained to continue text, not to obey it. Given
“Write a poem about the sea”, a base GPT-3 may continue with more similar instructions or an
unrelated paragraph. Instruction tuning changes the learned behaviour to “given an instruction,
produce a response that fulfils it”.
2. Generalization to unseen instructions: Training on hundreds or thousands of diverse task
types teaches the general skill of understanding instructions, so the model performs well zero￾shot on new tasks it was never trained on (FLAN showed strong zero-shot gains on unseen task
clusters).
3. Less prompt engineering: Users can state what they want directly, without carefully crafted
few-shot examples.
4. Response format and style: The model learns to give complete, well-structured, concise
answers, follow format constraints (lists, word limits, JSON), and use a conversational turn
structure.
5. Foundation for alignment: Instruction tuning (SFT) is the first stage of RLHF; combined
with RLHF (InstructGPT), outputs become more helpful, truthful and less toxic. The 1.3B
InstructGPT was preferred by humans over the 175B GPT-3.
6. Scales well: Gains increase with the number of tasks and model size (Flan-PaLM), and including
CoT examples in the instruction data also improves reasoning.

(a) Four challenges in deploying the LLM
1. Hallucination and factual accuracy: The LLM may confidently invent wrong information –
non-existent policies, wrong prices, incorrect refund rules or order statuses. In customer support
this damages trust and may cause legal or financial liability. The base model also does not know
company-specific or up-to-date information.
2. Inference latency and scalability: Autoregressive generation produces one token at a time; a
300-token reply from a large model can take several seconds. Under peak traffic, requests queue
up, increasing waiting time. Long conversation histories increase the prompt length and the
KV-cache memory.
3. High computational cost: Large models need expensive GPUs (e.g. a 70B model needs ≈ 140
GB in FP16, i.e. multiple GPUs), or the organisation pays per token for an API. Cost grows
with traffic, prompt length and output length.
4. Data privacy and security: Queries contain personal data (names, addresses, order and
payment details). This must comply with data-protection laws (e.g. GDPR, India’s DPDP Act).
There are also risks of prompt injection or jailbreaks, leaking internal instructions or other
customers’ data.
5. Other challenges (additional): maintaining context over multi-turn conversations and context￾window limits; consistency of brand tone; handling ambiguous, angry or out-of-scope queries and
knowing when to hand over to a human agent; multilingual users; keeping knowledge updated;
bias and toxic outputs; monitoring and evaluation of quality in production.

The three goals pull against each other; improving one usually worsens at least one other:

Homework: LLM and its Application – Solutions Page 27
1. Quality vs latency: Larger models (e.g. 70B) give more accurate, fluent and context-aware
answers, but each token requires more computation, so time-to-first-token and time per token
increase. Techniques that improve quality – retrieval (RAG), long context, chain-of-thought,
self-verification – add more tokens and steps, increasing latency further. Smaller models respond
faster but make more mistakes.
2. Quality vs cost: Inference cost is roughly proportional to (model size) × (input + output
tokens). A large model needs more and costlier GPUs (or a higher API price per token). Using
fewer/smaller GPUs, aggressive quantization (INT4) or shorter answers reduces cost but can
lower accuracy.
3. Latency vs cost: Low latency at peak traffic requires more GPU replicas kept running (often
under-utilised at off-peak hours), which raises cost. Large batching improves GPU utilisation
and lowers cost per query, but each request may wait longer for its batch, increasing latency.
4. Approximate quantitative view: Generation time ≈ time-to-first-token + (number of output
tokens × time per token). Time per token grows with model size, and memory needed ≈
parameters × bytes per parameter + KV cache. Halving precision (FP16 → INT8) halves
weight memory and often speeds decoding with only small quality loss.
5. Balancing for this chatbot: The objective is the smallest/cheapest configuration that meets the
accuracy target and a latency target (e.g. first token in under 1 s). Typical balance: a medium￾size, fine-tuned model with RAG for accuracy; quantization and batching for cost; streaming
responses so users see text immediately; routing only hard queries to a larger model.
(c) Three measures to improve efficiency and reliability
1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with guardrails (reliability): Store FAQs,
product manuals, policies and order information in a vector database. For each query, retrieve
the most relevant passages and include them in the prompt, instructing the model to answer
only from this context and cite it. This grounds answers in up-to-date company knowledge, re￾duces hallucination, and avoids frequent re-training. Add input/output guardrails: PII masking,
prompt-injection filtering, content moderation, and confidence checks that escalate to a human
agent when the answer is uncertain or the query is sensitive (refunds, complaints).
2. Model optimization – fine-tuning a smaller model, quantization and distillation (ef￾ficiency): Fine-tune a smaller open model (e.g. 7B–13B) on the company’s past support con￾versations using LoRA/QLoRA, or distil a large model into a small one. Apply INT8/INT4
quantization to reduce memory (e.g. 7B: 14 GB in FP16 → ≈ 3.5 GB in INT4) and increase
speed, so the model fits on a single GPU with good domain accuracy.
3. Efficient serving infrastructure – caching, batching and autoscaling (efficiency and
reliability):
• Response/semantic caching: Many support questions repeat (“Where is my order?”, “How
do I reset my password?”). Cache answers for frequent or semantically similar queries and
return them instantly without calling the LLM.
• Optimized inference engines: vLLM/TensorRT-LLM/TGI with continuous batching, Page￾dAttention for the KV cache, prefix caching of the long system prompt, and streaming of
tokens to the user.
• Query routing: Simple intents handled by a small model or rules; only complex queries go
to a larger model.
• Autoscaling and load balancing: Add/remove GPU replicas according to traffic to handle
peaks without paying for idle capacity; fallback to a backup model or human on failure.
4. Continuous monitoring and evaluation (additional): Log latency, cost per query, resolu￾tion rate, escalation rate and user feedback (thumbs up/down); regularly evaluate answers on a
